title: High throughput method to determine the surface activity of antimicrobial polymeric materials
author: van Rensburg, Laubscher, et al.

steps.title: Obtain test and control disks
steps.instruction: Place each solid‑surface sample containing the antibiotic of interest and a cellulose disk without antibiotic (growth control) in separate sterile holders ready for inoculation.

steps.title: Inoculate disks with bacterial suspension
steps.instruction: Add 10 µL of a bacterial culture adjusted to 1.4 × 10⁷ cells · mL⁻¹ (equivalent to 5 × 10⁵ cells · cm⁻²) onto the surface of each disk.

steps.title: Incubate inoculated disks
steps.instruction: Incubate the inoculated disks for 24 h at 37 °C in a humidity chamber to limit evaporation.

steps.title: Recover cells from disks
steps.instruction: After incubation, transfer each disk together with the overlying culture into a microcentrifuge tube and add 1.00 mL of phosphate‑buffered saline (PBS).

substeps.instruction: Vortex the tube for 60 s to dislodge any surviving cells from the surface.

steps.title: Serial dilution and plating
steps.instruction: Perform a serial dilution of the vortexed suspension as required, then plate appropriate dilutions onto agar plates.

steps.title: Incubate agar plates
steps.instruction: Incubate the plated agar at 30 °C for 20–24 h.

steps.title: Count colonies and calculate log reduction
steps.instruction: Count colony‑forming units (CFU) on each plate. Calculate the log reduction for each antibiotic‑containing material using the equation Log reduction = log₁₀(A/B), where A is the CFU count from the control (cellulose disk) and B is the CFU count from the antibiotic‑containing material.

description: The study represents a proof-of-concept method for a range of solid surfaces with different active compounds thus the antibiotics were selected to represent a wide range of antimicrobial agents with different modes of action. The activity of each of the antibiotics was not the focus of the study, but they merely served as test compounds in the creation of model antimicrobial materials used to compare the three methods of activity determination. Five antibiotics were chosen to represent different classes, namely gentamicin (aminoglycoside), ampicillin (penicillin), bacitracin (cyclic branched peptide), gramicidin S (cyclic antibiotic peptide) and tetracycline (polyketide). They differ in size, chemistry (water solubility), mode of action and target(s). By extension, these differences influence the rate of activity and type of activity, which will highlight shortcomings within each of the two existing methods compared with our new method based on the ability of the assays to detect the activity of different antimicrobial compounds.
